en: The *Buddha-bhāṣita Sarvatra-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. The Buddha said:
"When a practitioner of the Way walks the path, if a mind of anger arises, they should immediately restrain themselves; they should restrain [it]."
To contemplate what is wholesome is the practice of a practitioner of the Way.

If one bestows wealth or profit, upon obtaining it, one should immediately reckon it as impermanent; not to commit offenses through the body means not committing the offenses of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct—this is what is meant by "not committing offenses through the body."
One who has eliminated anger neither speaks it with the mouth nor conceives it with the mind; this is what is meant by one who has eliminated the deeply resonant sound within the mind of anger.
It is like a person who commits a theft and says:
"What you have done is utterly disgraceful."
"This is what is meant by 'the sound of profound depth within the mind.
The Buddha said:

"'The sequential order of flavors' refers to when one consumes food, one harmonizes it externally and internally discerns its flavors so as not to err; this is what is meant by the sequential order of flavors."

The reason by which a bodhisattva attains this knowledge is that in previous lives, whatever he consumed, he first offered to his parents and to practitioners of the Way before eating it himself; for this reason, he has attained these thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva attains the four fearlessnesses by means of four things:
first, that which one knows oneself, one also desires others to know it all.”
Second, teaching others without weariness;
third, maintaining an impartial mind without concealment;
fourth, preaching the sutras for others without later regret.
These are the four matters.
By means of these same four matters, the Buddha also attains the four fearlessnesses:
first, speaking in accordance with the Dharma;
Second, not accepting the property of others;
third, equanimity of mind;
fourth, the full observance of the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are four fearlessnesses:
first, speaking according to reality;"
Second, having nothing for which one feels attachment;
third, the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery;
fourth, not engaging in disputes with others.
“There are three causes and conditions for the radiance upon the crown of the Buddha’s head:
first, lighting lamps as an offering to Buddhist temples;
second, delighting in and cherishing the illuminated scriptures.”
Third, to resolve the doubts and knots of people.
"The Buddha raises his right hand for four reasons:
first, because wicked people lack gratitude and reciprocity;..."
Second, because virtuous people are capable of reciprocity;
third, through manifest instruction;
and fourth, by telling others not to commit evil.
"When the Buddha raises his right hand, there are four causes and conditions:
first, he wishes to cause all people of the ten directions to come and study the Way, following his intention;
second, he wishes to show people that because of the merit he has practiced, he has now attained this mark."
Third, he exhorts others to all uphold the precepts;
fourth, his deportment is naturally so because he does not wish to see the evil conduct of others; for these reasons, he raises his right hand in all instances.
“There are three reasons why the Buddha does not wear shoes:
first, to cause practitioners to have few desires;
second, to manifest the wheels on the soles of his feet.”
Third, it causes those who see him to rejoice.
There are three reasons why the Buddha’s feet leave the ground four inches when he walks:
first, because he sees insects and ants on the ground; [the other two reasons follow].
Second, because there are growing grasses on the ground;
third, because he manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), desiring to cause people’s minds to rest upon the Buddha’s conduct.
There are three causes and conditions for the ground of the Buddha’s conduct being level regardless of its natural elevations and depressions:

First, in his former practices, he cultivated the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni) with the desire to bring peace and security to all beings. Since the earth rests upon water and there are spirits within the water, even insects and ants that came under the Buddha’s feet all attained peace and shared a single intention. For this reason, the low became high and the high became low.
Second, when the devas and spirits performed meritorious deeds to prepare the ground for the Buddha, the uneven terrain was leveled.

Third, while the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he cleared paths and constructed bridges to ferry people across; because he thereby obtained merit, the high and low became perfectly level, desiring that the minds of men should likewise be so.
“The Buddha does not fly through the air for four reasons:
first, to exhort his disciples to practice with diligence;
second, to cause his disciples to listen to the sutras.”
Third, to repay the kindness of past lives;
fourth, to manifest signs—therefore, he does not fly through the air.

"When the Buddha was in the world, devas, spirits, nāgas, and humans all came to the Buddha’s dwelling to hear the sutras, numbering in the hundreds and thousands of layers; whether walking or sitting, those in front and behind all beheld the Buddha’s face."

Why is this? Because in his previous lives, the Buddha’s speech was consistent and without contradiction; therefore, there is no one who does not see the face of the Buddha. When people lie down, they all turn their heads toward where the Buddha lies, out of reverence for the Buddha.
"When the Buddha first attained the Way, he did not eat for seven days; there were four causes and conditions for this:
first, he was so mindful of the Way that he forgot about food;
second, his single-mindedness rendered him free from hunger."
Third, to be joyful and free from craving;
fourth, not to dwell upon sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—
these are the four.
It is the same when one wishes for others to listen to the sutras.
Within the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, neither dust nor water adheres, nor does external grime adhere; this is due to two causes and conditions:
first, because he does not dwell upon the evils of any person.
Second, seeing that all people possess desire, he wishes to extinguish it.
As for the Buddha again washing his *kāṣāya*: external impurities do not adhere, yet internal ones do; because there is a body, there is impurity.

Why is this? Because external conduct has already been exhausted, defilements do not adhere to the exterior; because internal conduct is not yet exhausted, defilements do adhere. Since there is still a body, the interior is not yet exhausted; because the body functions as the vehicle for transgression, one does not begrudge even life or limb.
Why is this? It is because they further cherish their lives, for it is by means of life that one attains the Way.
"The Sūtra on Eight Billion Myriad Causes and Conditions" taught by the Buddha thoroughly cures the three illnesses of human beings:
First, greed and lust;
second, anger and hatred;
third, ignorance and delusion.
These three matters are divided into six; therefore, one should use the six *āyatanas* (decays) to treat the three illnesses.
The reason why the sūtras are numerous is like a person who takes medicine but whose illness does not subside; they must then take other medicines.
The Buddha said:

"Human minds have many facets; because they change rapidly, there are many sutras. These are taught according to one's disposition as a means of treatment, for the purpose of bringing about swift liberation.
"Even though the Buddha has attained the Way, he still possesses the three ailments and six anxieties."
The six sorrows refer to the sorrows of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The three ailments refer to the mind, intellect, and consciousness being plagued by apprehension and reception.

If even the Buddha, who has already attained the Way, possesses such sorrows and ailments, how much more so for others whose calamities and offenses are not yet exhausted and thus cannot transcend the world, or whose Buddha-deeds are not yet complete and thus cannot transcend the world?
“The Buddha relinquished twenty years of his remaining lifespan for three reasons:
first, because worldly people are attached to their physical bodies;
second, because that which he was to teach had already been completed.”
Third, because he feared that evil persons might slander him and thereby incur heavy retribution, he entered parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha departs from the world, he does not depart by means of his body, nor does he depart by means of his mind; it is simply for the sake of the extinction of suffering.
"Earth, water, fire, wind, and space are always present in the world without interruption.
There are three causes and conditions for the Buddha’s cremation of his body after passing into nirvana:
first, because it would otherwise decay and rot;"
Second, because insects and moths are born therein;
third, because people who bring offerings of incense and flowers obtain merit thereby.
"As for the five-colored light issuing from the Buddha’s mouth when he smiles, there are five causes and conditions: [as follows...]"
First, it was because he wished for people to have something to ask, so that they might derive benefit from what was asked;
second, it was because he feared people would say that the Buddha did not know how to smile;
third, it was to manifest light from within his mouth.
Fourth, he laughs at those who lack sincerity;
fifth, he laughs at Arhats who dwell in emptiness yet fail to attain the Bodhisattva path.
That the light returns and enters through the crown of his head signifies that he intends to reveal the Great Illumination to future generations.
When the Buddha was about to depart from the world, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All people in this world shall surely receive blessings from the Buddha.
Now that the Buddha is departing from the world, from whom shall the people of the world receive blessings?"
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Although I have transcended the world and departed, the sūtras and the Dharma shall remain."
Furthermore, there are four causes and conditions through which one may obtain merit:
first, when animals have nothing to eat, providing them with fodder so that they may survive;
second, seeing a person afflicted by illness who has no one to care for them, one should provide for and support them so that they may attain peace and security.
Third, one should protect and care for those who are poor and solitary;
fourth, one should provide for and look after those who practice meditation and contemplate the Way alone, having no food or clothing—
these are the four matters.
If one gives with a mind of pure benevolence, the merit obtained is equal to that of a Buddha, without any difference.
At that time, his body was in total pain, and he desired to pass away from this world.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"There are three reasons for one to preach the sutras:
first, it is because people might not believe the words of other bhikṣus after the Buddha has passed away."
Second, he encourages his disciples' minds so that they may understand; for the Buddha even commanded the bhikṣus to preach the sūtras, let alone others.
Third, he manifests the merits of Śāriputra, fearing that other bhikṣus might become individually arrogant in their desire to preach the sūtras.
For this reason, the Buddha had Śāriputra preach this sutra.
After the Buddha had passed away from the world, the arhats collectively rebuked Ānanda, saying:
"When the Buddha was in the world and desired water, why did you not give it to him?"
All those in the ten directions shall attain liberation through the Buddha; why do you not entreat the Buddha to remain and not enter *parinirvāṇa*?

The Buddha wishes to exercise the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) to abide for one eon, or even a hundred eons, or even a thousand eons; why do you not exhort the Buddha to exercise these four bases of psychic power?
Ānanda said: "If it is as you say, does the Buddha lack self-mastery that he must depend upon my words?
Even if he were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, how could Maitreya possibly come down to become a Buddha?"
The Buddha’s original retinue of fellow practitioners of the Way numbered eight hundred million people, all of whom sought the bodhisattva path; yet only two attained the Way:
the first was Śākyamuni, and the second was Maitreya, while the remaining individuals attained the state of arhat or pratyekabuddha.

The Buddha’s forbearance exceeds that of the earth; his mind is more supple than water; his will is firmer than Mount Sumeru; his merit exceeds the waters of the ocean; and his wisdom surpasses empty space. For these reasons, he attained Buddhahood first!
The Buddha said:
"There are four causes and conditions why Maitreya does not descend:
first, there are times when his merit corresponds to that realm."
Second, the people here are coarse and incapable of receiving the sutras;
third, their merit is not yet fulfilled;
fourth, there are those in the world capable of expounding the sutras; for these reasons, Maitreya does not descend.
From now until then, there will remain five hundred and seventy million and sixty thousand years. During the time of Maitreya, the eyes of all people will see four thousand *li*.
That the people of Maitreya’s time can see four thousand *li* with their eyes is obtained through ten original causes and conditions;
the first is not obscuring the sight of others.
Second, not abandoning people's eyes;
third, not obscuring people's eyes;
fourth, not concealing people's virtues.
Fifth, not looking upon killing;
sixth, not looking upon stealing;
seventh, not looking upon sexual misconduct.
Eighth, not looking at private parts or the shortcomings of others;
ninth, not looking at various evil things;
tenth, lighting lamps in Buddhist temples.
These are the ten matters.
"The Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Arhat—these three persons share the same Dharma but differ in their practice:
the Buddha is one whose mind is awakened;..."
The Pratyekabuddha knows through the perception of causes and conditions;
the Arhat knows it through sitting in meditation.

The Pratyekabuddha perceives the characteristics of birth and death through causes and conditions, maintains self-restraint and does not dare to depart from his practice, and attains the Way by perceiving these causes and conditions; therefore, he is called a Pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha, in order to practice the universal path for the sake of delivering and liberating sentient beings, sought the state of a Pratyekabuddha.

A Pratyekabuddha once cut his own flesh to sustain five hundred people; he pierced his own neck with a wooden stake to contemplate the conditions of causality (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Seeing that blood was like water and that all phenomena were impermanent, he immediately attained the Way.

There was a Pratyekabuddha who, having previously practiced as a bodhisattva for five hundred kalpas, already possessed thirty of the marks on his body; he lacked only two marks that fell short of those of a Buddha. That he did not reach the state of a Buddha was because he lacked skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

"The Buddha has taught the matters of birth and death, the diligent suffering of the three evil realms; one with wisdom and understanding thereby attains arhatship, and though they have become an arhat, they are the most honored among them."

Why is this? Because during five hundred kalpas of practicing the bodhisattva path in previous lives, he possessed a compassionate heart and desired to deliver the people of the ten directions; therefore, although he has attained the wisdom of an arhat, he is able to understand the dialects of various regions.

When he first became an arhat, he was unable to realize on his own that he had been a bodhisattva in a previous life. The Buddha then spoke of the merits of a buddha and further explained the merits of an arhat; only then did he come to know the greatness of a buddha’s merits and regretted his [previous] desires, resolving to turn his mind toward attaining buddhahood.
The Buddha said:
"Having already attained the path of Arhatship, which cannot be turned back, he then repented, saying:
'How foolish was I to have specifically taken up the path of Arhatship!'"
The Buddha then explained his meaning:
"Your wisdom surpasses that of other arhats, yet your wisdom does not equal that of a Buddha.

An arhat severs suffering for himself but does not sever the suffering of others; a Buddha, through his original practice, severs suffering for himself and also severs the suffering of others. For this reason, they do not reach equality."
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, there are three phrases by which one fully knows the intentions of others: [text missing]"
First, coarse speech;
second, profound speech;
third, leading speech.

Having attained these three modes of speech, one perceives when there is a wholesome intention, perceives when there is an unwholesome intention, and perceives when there is a patient intention; through these three modes of speech, one fully knows the minds of others.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"In the space of a finger-snap, does the human mind undergo sixty cycles of birth and death?
The Buddha said:
“There are nine hundred and sixty births and deaths, which is not a great number; they essentially consist of three types of intentions:
wholesome intention, unwholesome intention, and sensual intention.

There are three hundred and twenty wholesome intentions, three hundred and twenty unwholesome intentions, and three hundred and twenty sensual intentions. Within the space of a finger-snap, these three intentions operate simultaneously, totaling nine hundred and sixty births and deaths.”
Excluding the three hundred and twenty wholesome mental states, there remain six hundred and forty mental states pertaining to birth and death.

When the Buddha and Śāriputra practiced the Sūtra of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment together, as for their wisdom being unequal, it is like the act of breathing: though both air enters and exits through all the pores, one who is capable of awareness perceives only the inhalation and exhalation of the breath through the nose.

That which the Buddha knows is entirely known through every pore; that which Śāriputra knows is like the size of a nostril. If one were to divide what Śāriputra knows into sixteen parts, the wisdom of all wise people throughout a single Buddha-world—a trichiliocosm with its suns, moons, and heavens—would not equal even one-sixteenth part of what Śāriputra knows.

If one were to divide the Buddha’s wisdom into sixteen parts, the total knowledge possessed by Śāriputra throughout an entire Buddha-world would not equal even one-sixteenth part of what the Buddha knows.
The practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment has three grades: there are the great thirty-seven factors, the middling thirty-seven factors, and the small thirty-seven factors.

If one’s intention is great, one attains the great intention; if the intention is middling, one attains the middling intention; if the intention is small, one attains the small intention. When one deeply and wondrously practices all thirty-seven factors in their entirety, one then penetrates them through and through.
Why is this? Because the correct divisions are sixteen, and humans originally possess sixteen mental faculties; thus the Buddha has distinguished them, and for this reason they are not the same.
Śāriputra understands the discourse on all dharmas—the timely speech, the protective speech, and the guarded speech—and so the Buddha then said to Śāriputra:
"Because one must not entrust improper speech to others.
Śāriputra’s original name was Upatiṣya. "Śāriputra! [the Buddha said.]
When a previous Buddha passes away from the world, there are three causes and conditions:
first, the exhaustion of his past karma;
second, the unwillingness of beings to witness the Buddha’s passing into parinirvāṇa.
"Third, there is nothing further to be delivered or liberated.
After Śāriputra had finished receiving alms-food from others and returned to the vihāra, he said that he must repay his debts:

"To sit in meditation and contemplate the Way is to repay one's debt; not contemplating the Way is to act as a debtor. Receiving offerings while in such a state is like having a debt that is not yet settled and yet taking on more; before one's previous offenses are exhausted, one now commits further transgressions."
The Buddha said:
"When one consumes the offerings of others, one must not fail to contemplate the Way; furthermore, one gains benefit for oneself and for all beings. For this reason, one ought to repay the debt.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernormal powers; Ānanda is foremost in learning; Rāhula is foremost in ethical discipline; and Aniruddha is foremost in the divine eye.”
The Buddha sent Maudgalyāyana to invite Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"Tie up my belt; I fear I shall not be able to bear its weight."
Maudgalyāyana then pulled at the belt; the sun, moon, earth, and heavens of the trichiliocosm all shook, yet he could not cause the belt to rise.
Śāriputra then thought to himself, "I shall go first to the place where the Buddha is," but Maudgalyāyana followed behind him and arrived before Śāriputra.
The Buddha knew that each of the two was foremost.
"Among all the bhikṣus in the worlds of the ten directions, there is none who maintains the precepts as Rāhula does.
There are four causes and conditions for Rāhula’s observance of the precepts:"
First, one thinks to oneself:
"I am a son of the Buddha.
Second, one claims to possess many lives.
Third, one should constantly reflect:
"I am a śramaṇa. Fourth, one should maintain the precepts with the constant desire to excel other bhikṣus.
“Śāriputra! Suppose one were to take a single bowl of water and place it in the ocean, stir and scoop within that water, and then go to retrieve that same water the following morning.
Śāriputra, if you are still capable of such a thing, how much more so the Buddha!”
When Maudgalyāyana was struck by someone, he did not fly away because he had not yet attained the power of the supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Why was he unable to employ the supernormal faculties?
Because his karmic retribution had not yet been exhausted.
The Buddha said:

"King Vītaśoka traveled as far as the Twelve Gates, yet he returned without knowing the six constituents within his own body. Though he could maintain his resolve to practice the Way, he did not know that the body gives rise to the mind and the mind gives rise to the body; he was unable to discern this."
Knowing that he could be delivered, the Buddha went to stay with him for the night; however, the king did not recognize him as the Buddha.
The Buddha asked:
"What dharma does the King practice? What path does he favor?"
His hair and body hair stood on end.
The Buddha then explained for him that the phenomena within his body were empty; thereupon, he attained the Way.
However, because he had not completely severed [the fetters], he did not attain arhatship.
The Buddha said:
"All practitioners should know that the mind is able to attain the Way.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, Mālikā studied the sūtras for twenty-four years; she attained the understanding of the five verses, was freed from defilements, cast them down and abandoned them, and no longer felt anxiety. Why was this so?"
In his past lives, he had personally seen five hundred Buddhas and was fully conversant with all the various sutras; yet, he kept the Way of the scriptures hidden and refused to teach others.
Later, after being ill for twenty-four days, he finally felt remorse as death approached and called out to people to instruct him.

Since there is this one blessing, we know that even five words [of instruction] yield such merit; how much more so when one fully teaches others, whereby the resulting merit and benefit become incalculable. (In another edition, "Li Man Tai" is written as "Zhu Li Pan Te.")
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Canna who fell ill. The Buddha sent Śāriputra to go and share his alms with him.
Śāriputra then questioned him:"
"Does your eye have any cognition?
Cāṇakya replied, "The eye has no cognition;
it merely sees forms. When consciousness arises, the body arises; when the affliction of disease arrives, there is illness, yet the body does not even know death."
"Suppose one dies; earth, water, fire, wind, and space shall all perish, and it is merely the consciousness that migrates to a new birth.
The Buddha sent Śāriputra on his almsround past the house of a courtesan. The woman then closed her door and began preparing the road, saying to Śāriputra:
"If you do not engage in sexual intercourse with me, you shall enter this great fire!"
Śāriputra replied, "I would rather enter this fire than engage in sexual misconduct with you; for such lust causes one to fall into the evil realms from which there is no escape."
The deva then descended to rescue him.
The Buddha said:
"It is simply that people cannot maintain the precepts; if they were able to maintain them, they would never worry about being struck by false paths."
The Buddha said:

"In the past, there was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation and practiced the Way. Nanda, the younger brother of the Buddha, became intoxicated from drinking wine and frequently went to his side to sing and play."
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha,
"I wish to avoid it and depart.
The Buddha said:
"There is no need; Nanda shall attain the fruit of the path this very day.
The Buddha then dispatched Ānanda to go to his house, with Mahākāśyapa following behind him.
Śāriputra preached the sutras for him, Maudgalyāyana displayed his supernormal powers, and Nanda was filled with joy; he immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
The Buddha said: "When a bhikṣu practices the Path, if he simply maintains a firm mind, why worry about not attaining the Path?"
When the bhikṣu heard these words spoken by the Buddha, his mind was gladdened and liberated, and he immediately attained arhatship.
The Buddha’s paternal cousin, named Sunakṣatra, had attended upon the Buddha for eight years and then thought to himself:
"I have traveled together with my brothers, yet he alone is handsome and possesses the thirty-two marks."
Thereupon, evil intent arose within him.

He followed behind the Buddha, sweeping away the Buddha’s footprints so that people would not see the marks of his feet; furthermore, among the people, he claimed that the Buddha lacked the Way and was merely someone who could win people over with his speech.
When Śāriputra and Ānanda heard this, they became sorrowful and unhappy.
The Buddha said, "Sunakṣatra did not speak ill of me; he was merely praising the Buddha’s merits."
"Among words, human intent is what matters, for human intent is often afflicted by many ailments.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Sunakṣatra did not deliberate; he was merely angry. Why did he not deliberate?"
"The Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks, radiant splendor, and supernormal powers; he merely subdues those of heterodox paths.
The Buddha repeatedly instructed and admonished Sunakṣatra, yet his words of true correctness were perceived by him as the incantations of heretics; for this reason, he became angry.
The Buddha had an elder sister who, being advanced in years, personally wove a *kāṣāya* from golden threads; she then presented it to the Buddha.
The Buddha would not accept it.
She spoke thus once more:
"May the Buddha, out of compassion for me, accept this so that I may obtain merit.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"Would you please accept it on my behalf?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Give this to the community of bhikṣus.
I too am part of the community of bhikṣus; it would not be right to give it to the multitude alone. This shall serve as a causal condition for future generations."
Those who meet one another with joy in this present life were all kinsmen or spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in previous lives.
How is this known? Because their minds are harmonized upon meeting.
The Buddha said:
"In the world, people treat one another with only thin kindness, not with thick kindness.
The Buddha said:
“The one who has served me as an attendant was named Māgandika; the next was named Sunakṣatra; and the next was Ānanda.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I am old and wish to have one person to attend upon me.”
Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, and the others each wished to attend upon the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted."
Mahākāśyapa and Maudgalyāyana, through meditative reflection, knew that the Buddha desired Ānanda; they then called out to Ānanda, saying:
"You shall serve as the Buddha's attendant."
Ānanda said, “I do not dare to attend upon the Buddha; I am unable to attend upon the Buddha.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"I cannot help but attend upon the Buddha.
Ānanda said, "Please allow me four things: [text truncated]"
First, I do not wish to receive clothing left over from the Buddha;
second, I do not use food left over from the Buddha;
third, if someone invites the Buddha and the bhikṣus do not go, I likewise shall not go.
"Fourth, when the Buddha sits in meditation and contemplates the Way, I shall attain mastery over entering and emerging [from samādhi].
The Buddha said, "Excellent! I grant you this wish."
Thereupon, because Ānanda was serving the Buddha, he alone was able to question the Buddha.
The three disciples of the Buddha—Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila—sat together and reflected upon seven matters:
first, that one who has few desires attains the Path, whereas one with many desires does not attain the Path;
Second, those who attain the Way through contentment do not attain it through lack of contentment;
third, those who attain the Way through diligence do not attain it through lack of diligence;
fourth, those who attain the Way by guarding against the six sense-bases so that they do not arise do not attain it if they fail to guard the six sense-bases and allow them to arise.
Fifth, one attains the Way by guarding oneself; one does not attain the Way by failing to guard oneself.
Sixth, one attains the Way by maintaining mindfulness; one does not attain the Way by failing to maintain mindfulness.
Seventh, one attains the Way through wisdom; one does not attain the Way by lacking wisdom.
They were together contemplating seven matters.
At that time, they were sixty *li* away from the Buddha.
While the Buddha was sitting in meditation, he immediately knew what the three men were thinking; he then shifted his intention and went to sit before the three men, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
I shall further tell you one more thing:”
"One who does not dwell on the household while seeking the Way will attain it; one who dwells on the household while seeking the Way will not attain it.
Thereupon, the three men rejoiced and immediately attained the state of Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What the human eye sees extends for four million two hundred thousand yojanas.
How is this known?
The sun and moon are four million two hundred thousand yojanas from the earth; since the human eye sees the sun and moon, it is by this that we know the extent of what the eye perceives."

In the vast and distant reaches of the ten directions, the suns and moons are hundreds of billions of times more numerous than the grains of sand in the great ocean; even by hundreds of billions of times, they cannot be calculated or known.

The merits and calamities resulting from the good and evil deeds performed by people—including the merits and calamities performed previously and subsequently—are beyond reckoning, numbering in the hundreds of millions.

All good and evil ultimately depend on the moment when life ends: those who commit evil encounter evil realms, while those who practice goodness attain good realms; both calamity and fortune are predetermined, and all such destinations are predetermined.
"If there are parents, brothers, wives, or children who attain the Way, they will simply cease [their worldly ties]; if they do not attain the Way, those ties will not be severed.
The Buddha said, "Devadatta merely teaches people to perform meritorious deeds, but does not teach them to practice the Way."
Those who follow the Buddha cultivate merit, maintain the precepts, and guard their minds, ceasing only upon attaining the Way.
Devadatta, however, conceived this thought in his own mind:

"I shall manifest my supernormal powers before King Ajātaśatru; when the king follows me, others will all follow as well. I shall then transform myself into a white elephant and enter and exit the palace alone."
He further transformed himself into a small child, peerlessly handsome, and climbed onto the king's lap; the king loved him dearly.

Seeing that Devadatta had acted in such a manner, the king’s mind came to regard Devadatta as superior to the Buddha. The king then followed whatever Devadatta said, and the king’s officials, subjects, and even those śramaṇas who had not yet attained the Way all followed the king to Devadatta’s place to inquire about matters.
Devadatta then went to where the Buddha was and said, "The Buddha is old; he need no longer teach his disciples.
Devadatta then summoned Śāriputra to leave, as well as the other śramaṇas to depart.
"Devadatta was deluded by greed and harbored such evil intent that he lost his supernormal powers.
The Buddha said, "The actions of a deluded person are inverted; they are not the way of the Buddhas' Dharma."
Devadatta thought to himself:
"I shall fly away; when people see me flying, they will all follow my example.
As he attempted to fly, he was suddenly unable to do so.

Devadatta was unable to realize that he had lost his supernormal powers (ṛddhi). At that time, there was a brahmin who cultivated an impartial mind; he descended from the first heaven and said to Śāriputra, "Devadatta has lost his supernormal powers."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Devadatta wishes to summon you, so as to cause you to incur further transgressions.
The Buddha then spoke to the deva, saying:
“Devadatta has not yet attained the supernormal powers; I knew he would lose them.
How much more so now?
The Buddha said:
"One should not be greedy; it was solely because of his greed that Devadatta lost his supernormal powers.
The Buddha said, "There are two types of Arhats: [those who have attained through effort and those who have attained naturally]."
The first was named Śrama; he worried that he had attained the Way and immediately desired to transcend the world and depart.
The second group, who followed and protected him, all attained liberation.

The Buddha and the Arhats together practiced the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma). It is like a lamp or a fire: the Buddha calculates and discerns how many matters there are, knowing their beginning and end, and by guarding against them, he extinguishes them.
The Arhat does not calculate from the root to the branches, but directly extinguishes them.
The Buddha is like one who climbs a tree from the root to the branches, discerning and knowing it all;
the practice of the Arhat is like one who goes from the branches back to the root.
Regarding that which proceeds from the beginning to the end, one calculates the beginning as empty;
yet for one who does not know emptiness, the Way cannot be attained.
The Buddha said:

“The Arhat possesses the flourishing aggregates (skandhas) yet lacks the five [defiled] aggregates; all that he has is manifest, yet he is merely unattached to it. He possesses form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet there is no birth-and-death.”
The Buddha said:
"An arhat maintains silence through cultivation, for having attained arhatship, there are three characteristics:
first, one no longer commits transgressions of body, speech, or mind;..."
Second, the extinction of the three poisons;
third, not seeking excellence in food and clothing, but merely extinguishing hunger and cold.
With these three causes and conditions, one is able to exercise mastery over transformations and remain unattached in mind.
"Because of the six decays (āsravas), one does not attain mastery.
The Buddha said:
"The mind should merely discern the six decays and should not be attached to them; if one is attached, one will not attain the Way."
The Buddha said:
"There are two causes and conditions by which an Arhat’s flight is made invisible to others:
first, the fear that people, upon seeing him, would offer excessive veneration."
"Second, I fear that wicked people might become jealous of me.
The Buddha said,
"Manifesting supernatural powers brings two further blessings:"
First, when people see him flying, they apply themselves with diligence to mindfulness of the Way;
second, by receiving offerings from people, he enables them to obtain great merit and utility;
for these reasons, he manifests supernatural powers.
"Because of mental joy, one obtains great merit.
The Buddha said,
"There was an Arhat named Gavāmpati who, having already attained the path of Arhatship, instead became a cowherd."
The disciple asked the Buddha,
"For what reason?
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu, in his previous lives, was a cow for seven hundred lifetimes; though he has now attained the Way in this life, the residual habits have not yet been exhausted.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"You should contemplate the impermanence of the body."
A certain bhikṣu then replied to the Buddha, saying:
"I contemplate impermanence; a person in this world can live at most fifty years.
The Buddha said:
"Do not speak such words.
Then another bhikṣu said,
"He must be about thirty years old."
The Buddha spoke again:
"Do not speak such words.
Then another bhikṣu said:
"It may be ten years.
The Buddha said,
"Do not speak such words."
Again, another bhikṣu said,
“One year would suffice.
The Buddha spoke again:
"Do not speak such words.
Then another bhikṣu said,
"One month would suffice."
The Buddha spoke again:
"Do not speak such words.
Then another bhikṣu said:
"It may be for one day," the Buddha replied. He spoke again:
"Do not say such words."
Again, another bhikṣu said:
"It may be done all at once.
The Buddha spoke again:
"Do not speak such words.
Another bhikṣu then said,
"It was but the space of a single breath."
The Buddha said, “It is so.
The Buddha said:
"If the exhaled breath does not return, one belongs to the next world; human life exists but between a single inhalation and exhalation.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "All of you should assemble and sit together;

you should speak only of the Dharma. Those who are unable [to do so] should quickly close their eyes and silence their voices, guarding their minds and listening well; through this, you may attain the Way."
When the bhikṣus heard these words spoken by the Buddha, they were filled with joy and their minds were liberated; they immediately attained the path of arhatship. The Buddha said:

"When a bhikṣu enters a person's house, he should be like a hand in the air, meeting no obstruction; his mind likewise should have no attachments. To hear what is pleasing to the ear is attachment; to hear what is displeasing to the ear is attachment."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If both the acceptable and the unacceptable are attachments, how can one attain the Way?
The Buddha said:
“The bhikṣus understand that emptiness is entirely without attachment; this accords with the practice of a bodhisattva.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were all filled with joy and exultation, and immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha said:
"There was a bhikṣu sitting in the mountains who sighed.
A man asked the bhikṣu:"
"You have entered the Way; why do you sigh?
The bhikṣu replied, "When I was in the hells, the five poisons caused me extreme pain."

Now that I have attained human birth and further encountered the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, yet I still fail to attain the Way; fearing death and returning once more to these evil realms, I sigh for this reason!
"Even for a bhikṣu, there is anxiety regarding worldly people, anxiety regarding the sūtras and precepts, and anxiety regarding his own person; thus, a wholesome mind cannot be maintained constantly.
When certain conditions arise, he may then think of his wife and children or of wealth; this constitutes falling into the evil realms."
The Buddha said:
"There was a bhikṣu who went to the house of an upāsikā for alms and preached the sūtra for her.
The upāsikā then knelt down with her knees on the ground and shed tears."
The bhikṣu preached the sūtra until midnight, yet the upāsikā remained kneeling without rising.
The bhikṣu said,
"In my travels preaching the sūtra, I have never seen anyone exert such diligence as this."
The upāsikā replied, “In my house there was a donkey that died at midnight while braying; that is why these tears have come forth.
The Buddha said:
"A person's preaching of the sutras does not lie in the quantity, but rather in whether they possess understanding and wisdom.
A certain bhikṣu, having heard the Buddha speak of this matter, went to question the Buddha, saying:
"Please teach me one essential dharma so that I may attain the Way."
The Buddha said, "Do not take what is not yours; take that which is yours.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu reflected within himself:
"All the myriad things in the world are not permitted to me; only the good is the property of this household.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have understood."
The Buddha said,
"To understand this is itself the Way.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, went to question him.
"Has Śāriputra attained this?
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra has attained it all."
The bhikṣu said,
"Śāriputra, why did you revile me and use your saṃghāṭī to wipe my face?
The Buddha said:
"Call Śāriputra here and question him.
Śāriputra said, "I had no ill intent;
the reason I reviled you was that I wished to cause you to practice patience."
"The reason he holds his *kāṣāya* robe to wipe his face is that he wishes to purify his eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This was performed by Śāriputra through his skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."
Thereupon, the bhikṣu rejoiced and immediately attained the path of arhatship.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, a certain man went to challenge a bhikṣu, saying:"

"If, upon the death of a person, consciousness, mindfulness, thought, and all that is known are extinguished, and when one practices the Path and attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that which is known is likewise extinguished—what is the difference between these two?
The bhikṣu replied: "In both cases there is extinction.

When a person dies and their life-force is exhausted, the spirit (*ātman*) is not extinguished; it is reborn according to its past conduct. However, because it is subtle and cannot be easily perceived, the results obtained differ: for those who do good, they ascend to heaven; for those who do evil, they enter the abyss. This is the difference."
The Buddha said:

“There was a bhikṣu who went to the house of an upāsikā for alms. Seeing that she was beautiful and upright, the bhikṣu gave rise to an improper thought, and because of this, he arose [from his seat].”
The upāsikā then took the food and gave it to him, but the bhikṣu departed, saying,
"I should not accept the offerings of others.
The upāsikā then replied to him:
"If she already has the intention to repent, you may accept her offering.
The upāsikā replied accordingly, and the bhikṣu then accepted it.
The Buddha said:
"Just as when a person perceives their own evil immediately, that transgression is extinguished;
so too, when a bhikṣu receives offerings, there is no transgression.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"If one can contemplate emptiness and control the mind for even as long as a finger-snap, one may attain the Way.
The Buddha said:
"There was a bhikṣu who, while sitting, attained concentration of mind."
There was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who saw that the seating area was uneven; he pulled [the person] up and showed him a comfortable place.
Later, this lay follower failed to attain peace and security for five hundred kalpas.
"Why is this? Because they have severed the mindfulness of the path.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"There is a discourse that says: 'Be careful not to interrupt it; the sin of interrupting a discourse is heavy and incalculable.
The Buddha said:
'There was a bhikṣu practicing the Path who attained the first dhyāna and said to himself:'"
"I have attained the path of the stream-enterer; by the merit of the first dhyāna, I shall be reborn in the seventh heaven above with a lifespan of one kalpa.
Having attained the second dhyāna, I reckon that I have attained the stage of once-returner.
By the merit of the third dhyāna, I shall be reborn in the fifteenth heaven above with a lifespan of eight kalpas."
"Having attained the four dhyānas, I reckoned to myself that I had become an arhat.
Why is it that I have not been reborn in the nineteenth heaven with a lifespan of sixteen kalpas?
Having said this, he then spoke again:
"The Buddha is a slanderer!
Immediately, he fell from heaven into hell; unaware that his celestial lifespan had ended, he was instantly subjected to the retribution of hell.

For example, it is like a person in the world who obtains rare treasures, but in a single day sets fire to them and burns them all away; so too, when a person gives rise to evil intentions, they recklessly burn away their wholesome roots. (In the various editions below the section on the Sakṛdāgāmin, the text regarding being born in heaven for a kalpa-long lifespan and attaining the third dhyāna has been omitted.)
The Buddha said:
"A person's good and evil follow one another; there is no way to escape them, except that by attaining the Way, one may leave the mundane world behind.
The Buddha said:
"There are five blessings in not eating after midday:
first, little lust;
second, little sleep; [and so forth]."
Third, one attains single-minded concentration;
fourth, there is no downward wind;
fifth, the body is peaceful and secure, and no illness arises.
Therefore, śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way know that they do not eat for the sake of merit.
There are three reasons for rinsing the mouth and washing:
first, it is out of fear of the filth beneath one's nails.
Second, scratching when it is pleasant to one's mind;
third, because of killing fleas and mosquitoes, one also desires to keep the mind pure and free from desire, so as not to defile the sutras—these [acts] merely serve to remove external impurities.

If one harbors evil thoughts in the mind and cannot eliminate them, for a student of the Way, the primary requirement is to take the purification of the mind as the foundation. The mind is the root of all phenomena; when the mind is upright, conduct becomes correct, and when conduct is correct, one accords with the Way.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a śrāmaṇera traveling with his teacher who saw gold on the ground; he then took it in silence and said to his teacher:"
"Traveling swiftly through this place, there is no one here; it is truly terrifying.
The teacher said, "It is simply because there is gold here that it makes you afraid."
Having discarded the gold and departed, he was no longer afraid.
His disciple then paid obeisance to his teacher and said:
"Because I was foolish and ignorant, I was previously anxious; now that it has been discarded, I am no longer apprehensive regarding this."
The Buddha told his disciples:
"A student who craves the Way is like a novice monk craving gold; why worry about not attaining the Way!
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“There was a bhikṣu practicing the Path who did not apply himself diligently when receiving the sūtras from his teacher.
His teacher instructed him to take several sheng of cow and horse dung and burn it; by nightfall, it was still not exhausted.”
The Master took a large rock and held it within the hell; when he burned it with fire, it immediately turned to ash.
His disciple was greatly terrified and knelt for a long time, asking the Master, "What kind of fire is this?"
The teacher said:
"If you do not read the scriptures and practice the Path, after death you shall enter hell; there the fires of hell will burn you without a moment's delay."
Thereupon, the bhikṣu was filled with fear and alarm, and he applied himself even more diligently.
Hearing one Āgama each day, he attained the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha said:
“Such is the skillful means of expedient power for delivering others.
The Buddha said:
“The Anāgāmin has three fetters:”
First, the fetter of delusion;
second, the fetter of worldly craving;
third, the fetter of views that have not yet been seen through and have not yet been exhausted.
The Anāgāmin is like the crest of a flame on a fire; though smoke arises, it cannot burn anything.
The Srotāpanna eliminates eighty-eight fetters;
the Sakṛdāgāmin eliminates seven fetters.
The Anāgāmin eliminates the three fetters;
the Arhat is free from all fetters.
The Srotāpanna attains the track of the Path; the Sakṛdāgāmin attains the Path by returning once more; the Anāgāmin does not return to this world; and the Arhat is no longer subject to attachment.
What is the track for attaining the Path? It is the recognition of suffering.

Worldly people do not recognize suffering; the *srotāpanna* recognizes suffering; the *sakṛdāgāmin* abandons its accumulation; the *anāgāmin* knows its exhaustion; and the *arhat* has completed the practice of the Path.
Having attained the stage of Srotāpanna, one must wait another hundred kalpas before attaining Arhatship. Why is this?

Because although one has been a Srotāpanna for a hundred kalpas, there remain ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) that have not been severed; thus, one does not attain Arhatship. A Srotāpanna merely worries about his own person and fears transgression, not daring to involve himself in worldly affairs; yet because he still possesses ten knots of doubt that are not resolved, he remains stationary due to this lack of resolution.
The five lower fetters that are abandoned by a srotāpanna are:
first, the fetter of sensual desire;
second, the fetter of ill will; [and so forth].
Third, the fetter of views and conduct;
fourth, the fetter of attachment to precepts and merit;
fifth, the fetter of doubt. Furthermore, from the six heavens below up to the world of desire, the craving for the body, malice, and doubt regarding one's vows constitute the lower fetters.

Regarding the stream-enterer who perceives causes and conditions: this refers to one who does not transgress the five precepts; even when facing death, they do not transgress them at the time of death. Others, seeing the urgency of the situation, all transgress the five causes and conditions.

The *srotāpanna* severs the old and receives the new; the *arhat* severs both the new and the old entirely. The Bodhisattva exhausts past transgressions, and upon the exhaustion of transgressions, attains the Way. Only then does one know that all things are impermanent, suffering, and empty, and that there is neither self nor path. When practicing the Way, the practitioner of the Way should not have any attachments.

By practicing the path of a srotāpanna, one attains the fruit of srotāpanna; by practicing the path of a sakṛdāgāmin, one attains the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin; by practicing the path of an anāgāmin, one attains the fruit of anāgāmin; by practicing the path of an arhat, one attains the fruit of arhat; by practicing the path of a pratyekabuddha, one attains the fruit of pratyekabuddha; by practicing the path of a bodhisattva, one attains the state of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"Whatever a practitioner does according to their own inclination, they will immediately receive its retribution, just as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound.
The Buddha said:
"The bowl has four names:
first, it is called 'that which does not provide food';
second, it is called 'precept'."
The third is called "receiving," and the fourth is called "following.
Thus, one attains merit free from defilement; one should receive this merit and maintain the bowl while establishing the precepts, with no evil thoughts in the mind.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding why Arhats do not eat meat: if one calculates from head to foot the various parts of an animal, each has its own specific name, but there is no such thing as a 'name for meat'."
The Pratyekabuddha considers that what is produced by the essence of the fundamental [elements] is impure; therefore, he does not eat meat.
The Buddha considers that all under heaven is empty and non-existent: that which exists perishes, and having perished, it is born again, ultimately returning to emptiness; thus, it is non-existent.
The disciples, having heard this sutra, rejoiced, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Thus concludes the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Various Places*.
